column4: After the self-sufficient man's claim in 96:6-7, this ayah says the return is to the Lord, limiting the imagined independence that the section identifies.
The repeated “Have you seen?” asks whether the praying servant is upon guidance, placing his inward direction against the one who forbids him.
The next question asks whether that servant enjoins piety, giving the prayerful figure an ethical action that contrasts with obstruction.
The verse says they hide themselves from people but cannot hide from Allah, then describes their night plotting; it names the unseen divine audience behind the section's public display.
After the mosque built for harm, disbelief, and division, this ayah forbids standing there and favors the mosque founded on piety, where people seek purification.
It contrasts a building founded on piety and Allah's approval with one on a crumbling bank, making the true foundation of an outward religious structure visible.
This ayah describes the stingy person who sees himself as self-sufficient, closely joining the section's 96:7 self-perception to its refusal of aid.
It adds that this person denies al-husna, completing the specific pairing of self-sufficiency, denial, and withholding.
The covenant joins kindness to orphans and the needy, good speech, and prayer; its next clause says most turned away, gathering the section's care and worship concerns.
After the speaker's destructive conduct in 2:205, this ayah says that when told to fear Allah, pride drives him into sin, exposing the stance beneath his pleasing words.
Asked about orphans, the reply makes their reformation best and says Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer, linking outward treatment to hidden intent.
After the concealment from people but not Allah in 4:108, this ayah contrasts arguing for someone in worldly life with who will argue for him before Allah on the Resurrection.
The speaker is told to say that his prayer, rites, life, and death are for Allah; prayer's stated audience is therefore the opposite of the people sought by show-offs.
The command to take adornment at every place of prayer sets a boundary: visible clothing can accompany worship, while the section's concern is the audience and motive behind display.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each said to be questioned, giving the section's named eye-sight and inward insight a concrete accountability before God.
The verse says that possession of the Lord's mercy-treasures would make people withhold for fear of spending, a specific parallel to refusing even small aid.
Giving relatives, the needy, and travelers their due is joined to seeking Allah's face, pairing care for the vulnerable with the section's question of audience.
The believers are described as bowing and prostrating while seeking Allah's bounty and pleasure, with a mark of prostration on their faces: outward appearance here accompanies sincere devotion.
At judgment the cover is removed and sight becomes sharp, a specific boundary to the section's call to see a person's reality before the veil is lifted too late.
This ayah condemns people who are stingy and urge others to be stingy, turning the section's absent encouragement to feed the poor into active encouragement of withholding.
When good reaches a person, he withholds; this names the disposition behind the section's refusal of small assistance.
The next ayah begins the exception, “except those who pray,” whose steadiness and known share for the needy are described in 70:23-25.
The contrasting person gives and fears Allah, joining generosity to an inward orientation rather than an audience.
He confirms al-husna, completing the good person's motive in the passage that turns in 92:8-9 to stinginess and denial.
The next ayah says Allah eases him toward ease, completing the consequence for the giver in contrast with 92:10.
After describing stinginess and denial in 92:8-9, this ayah says the way is eased toward hardship, completing that contrary path.
The verse says spending is for the givers themselves and that they spend seeking only Allah's face, repeating the section's contrast between divine aim and human notice.
It warns those who withhold Allah's bounty not to think it good, and says it will be a burden on the Day of Resurrection, extending the section's hidden withholding into judgment.
